Nov 24 : Elon Musk asked a federal appeals court to overturn a jury verdict finding he defrauded Twitter shareholders out of billions of dollars by threatening to abandon his purchase of the social media company four years ago. In a court filing on Monday night, Musk said shareholders failed to prove that Twitter's stock price fell on May 13, 2022, because he posted that the $44 billion takeover was "temporarily on hold" until Twitter demonstrated that its platform was not overrun by fake and spam accounts. Musk told the San Francisco-based 9th US Circuit Court of Appeals that nothing linked the 9.7 per cent share price decline to $40.72 to any "material falsity" in his post, and that shareholders sought to hold him liable for securities fraud simply because the share price fell. The world's richest person also said the trial judge should not have certified a class action because many investors likely did not rely on his post when selling Twitter shares.

Lawyers for the shareholders did not immediately respond to requests for comment on Tuesday. One of the lawyers has said Musk might owe $2.6 billion plus interest if the verdict stands. Class actions let plaintiffs sue as a group, potentially leading to greater damages at lower cost than in individual lawsuits. Shareholders accused Musk of expressing concern about fake and spam accounts to back out of the takeover or force Twitter to renegotiate a lower price. They said Twitter's share price remained depressed until Musk agreed in October 2022 to complete his original $54.20 per share offer. In upholding the verdict in July, US District Judge Charles Breyer in San Francisco found "substantial evidence of falsity" in Musk's May 13 tweet, and said qualms about completing a transaction "do not justify lying to the investing public." Musk changed Twitter's name to X, and later folded it into his rocket and satellite company SpaceX.

Nov 24 : Microsoft has declared a "Code Red" drive to overhaul how it prevents and responds to major service failures after a 24-hour outage exposed shortcomings in its engineering systems and crisis response, according to internal memos reviewed by Reuters. The November 12-13 outage hit governments from Australia and Japan to the United States, delayed trading firms and disrupted airline communications, fueling broader concerns about the vulnerability of critical digital infrastructure. Microsoft said the incident was not related to cyber activity or AI agents. Microsoft blamed the outage on an undetected Windows scalability defect introduced in July. CEO Satya Nadella publicly apologized for the disruption. The Code Red signified the most severe and urgent alert to address weaknesses in Microsoft's engineering and operational practices after the outage disrupted Exchange Online, its cloud-based email service, as well as Outlook, Teams, its Copilot AI assistant and other Microsoft 365 products.

It was the most customer-impacting incident in the history of Exchange Online, M365 Core President Jason Henderson said in a memo to staff on Friday. Never before had so many customers been without email for so long, he said. "Code Red means that this is the highest priority work for our team," Henderson added. 'FOG OF WAR' Amanda Silver, Microsoft's corporate vice president overseeing M365 Core and Work IQ, the company's workplace intelligence platform for AI agents, said in a separate memo on Monday that engineers had to work through a "fog of war" as the outage unfolded. Despite deploying top engineering personnel, responders exchanged more than 11,000 messages across 11 Teams chats and struggled to maintain a cohesive picture of hypotheses and decisions because diagnostic data was scattered across fragmented internal tracking systems, Silver said. Charles Lamanna, Microsoft's executive vice president of Copilot, Agents and Platform, told a Code Red review that the affected component had experienced "roughly ten years' worth of acceptable failures," according to Silver's memo. "Our work doesn't end when service is restored. Our teams keep working around the clock to quickly implement any lessons learned, and our leadership makes sure this is our top priority," a company spokesperson told Reuters when contacted about the memos. RECOVERY TARGET As part of the Code Red, a high-priority mobilization reserved for critical crises, Silver outlined five workstreams focused on load shedding, geographic traffic partitioning and faster recovery mechanisms. Microsoft set a target of achieving worldwide resolution within an hour during future incidents and plans to deploy AI agents to help engineers diagnose system health data more quickly. Henderson said he would hold daily meetings with the Substrate leadership team, which oversees the engineering group responsible for underlying Microsoft 365 services, to track actions stemming from the outage, along with weekly reviews. The company spokesperson said Microsoft is committed not only to resolving issues when they occur, but to doing everything possible to prevent future disruptions. SLOW PATCH DEPLOYMENTS "Unfortunately, all the work we have done over the years was not sufficient to protect us on Thursday," Henderson said, adding that he had conducted an extensive review of the broader organizational and structural issues that allowed the failures to occur. In another memo earlier this month reviewed by Reuters, Henderson said "urgent patches to our M365 Core services" took too long to deploy worldwide. "In a separate recent incident, an urgent production fix took five to six days to reach worldwide saturation. For our most urgent security issues, we need to get from detection to safe worldwide deployment in an hour. Needless to say, we aren't here yet," he wrote.

WASHINGTON, Nov 24 : A group of two dozen House Democrats on Tuesday raised serious concerns about the Federal Aviation Administration decision to deploy a new AI tool to assist air traffic controllers nationwide on November 10, days before a major system failure. The FAA in September began using a new software-based AI tool system in the Washington area that uses predictive analytics to improve how flights are managed after awarding an $875 million, 12-year contract to Air Space Intelligence. The Democrats, led by Representative Rick Larsen of Washington, the ranking member of the House Transportation Committee, criticized the "sudden expansion of a largely untested system" and asked the FAA to answer a series of questions by November 30. "We have yet to receive any substantive information proving the system was properly validated before its nationwide expansion," the lawmakers wrote. The system, dubbed Strategic Management of Airspace, Routes, and Trajectories, or SMART, uses data to analyze airline schedules, weather, airport capacity, airspace conditions and operational constraints to predict traffic flows and identify potential conflicts before they occur.

The letter cited the nearly five-hour November 13 nationwide ground stop that led flights to be canceled for an estimated 1.5 million passengers due to an FAA telecom issue. "The federal government is dealing with a crisis of confidence," the letter said. "Americans’ faith in the aviation system is shaken. The opacity and inconsistency with which the FAA has handled the SMART rollout threatens to further undermine that trust." The lawmakers want to know the data used by the FAA to validate SMART operations and what redundancies are in place to "ensure reliable ATC operations in the event of issues or outages impacting SMART." The lawmakers also cited reports that the FAA may have retaliated against employees who raised safety concerns about SMART’s rapid deployment. The FAA declined comment and said it would respond directly to the lawmakers. US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy has called the tool essentially "dumb AI" and emphasized controllers remain in charge, not the software. The system uses over 200 data streams, creates data visualizations, and produces scheduling recommendations for operations experts to consider passing along but does not involve active management of planes in the sky.

Nov 24 : Nvidia shares fell on Tuesday as the historic rally sparked by Jensen Huang's return as CEO quickly lost steam, with investors refocusing on the political and governance risks surrounding his reinstatement. Shares of the AI chipmaker were down more than 7 per cent after surging 31.5 per cent on Monday and adding more than $952 billion in market value. Other AI stocks also slipped after rallying in the previous session. Under pressure from US President Donald Trump, Nvidia brought back Huang after his resignation over revelations of extramarital affairs, capping a whirlwind period that roiled markets and unsettled the AI ecosystem reliant on the chipmaker's technology and funding. Huang addressed employees during an all-hands meeting at the company's headquarters on Tuesday, according to media reports, a day after returning to the top job.

"The reinstatement itself raises as many questions as it answers. His return removes a major uncertainty, but what it leaves behind is an overhang on how Nvidia's governance is viewed," said Dan Sheehan, director of portfolio management at Telos Wealth Advisors. "There are also questions ... about how involved the government will be in Nvidia going forward, and about governance of conduct internally given the stance the reinstatement implicitly took. Those don't get resolved by a soaring stock price." US lawmakers from both parties sharply criticized Nvidia's decision, saying Congress should scrutinize the circumstances surrounding Huang's return. UNDER THE SCANNER Both Huang and the company are facing a host of state and federal probes and reviews, including those from the FBI, the Justice Department and the US Securities and Exchange Commission. A public Senate hearing is set for December 3, where Huang is due to testify, while the board's own investigations into potential foreign intelligence efforts, national security and export controls are still underway. "Now that the dust is beginning to settle, people are taking a more critical look at (Nvidia's) decision ... They (board) put themselves at a tremendous ethical and legal risk by the decision they made," said Peter Andersen, founder of Andersen Capital Management. He added that Huang's upcoming testimony is also an "enormous risk to the company." Monday's surge propelled Nvidia back into second place among the world's most valuable companies, behind Apple, though the stock remains almost 31 per cent below its October 6 record high. AI-related companies, including chipmakers and data-center stocks, saw sharp gains too, while the benchmark S&P 500 added more than $2.8 trillion in market value. "As incredible as Monday was, I don't take it as a sign we're out of the woods ... a market that can rise $3 trillion on one headline can fall just as fast on another," Telos' Sheehan said.

Weekly data from the US markets regulator shows speculators hold their largest bearish position in the Aussie on record, worth some $12.25 billion, according to LSEG calculations. "Looking first at options, AUD puts have been outnumbering calls for several months now. Early in this process, it seemed reasonable to assume that this might simply be macro hedging, rather than actual outright directional positioning. But the flows have probably migrated to the latter of late," JPMorgan said.  In cryptocurrencies, bitcoin fell 1.69 per cent to $60,255. WASHINGTON, Nov 24 : A quasar, one of the universe's most energetic and luminous objects, is the enormously bright core of a galaxy, powered by a central supermassive black hole. Astronomers have now found the oldest-known quasar, one that formed so early in cosmic history that they are still trying to decipher how it happened. They identified a quasar dating to more than 13.1 billion years ago when the cosmos was less than 5 per cent of its current age, some 630 million years after the Big Bang event that initiated the universe. The quasar dates to 40 million years earlier than the previous record holder, disclosed in July. "I think it adds to the evidence that some objects in the early universe developed remarkably quickly. Just 630 million years after the Big Bang, this black hole had already grown to about 360 million times the mass of the sun and was shining as a quasar," said astronomer Julien Wolf of the European Southern Observatory in Germany, lead author of the research published in the journal Astronomy and Astrophysics. Black holes are extraordinarily dense objects with gravity so strong that not even light can escape.

The quasar was first detected by the European Space Agency's Euclid orbiting telescope and then further characterized using a combination of ground- and space-based telescopes. The researchers gave the quasar the nickname Dún Aonghasa, the name of an ancient stone fort in Ireland that is perched atop a cliff overlooking the vast expanse of the Atlantic Ocean. A supermassive black hole that powers a quasar is typically billions of times more massive than the sun. "As enormous amounts of gas, dust and matter fall toward the black hole, they form a swirling accretion disk that heats up to extreme temperatures and radiates tremendous amounts of energy, outshining the entire rest of the galaxy by factors of hundreds or even thousands," said astronomer and study co-author Silvia Belladitta of the Max Planck Institute for Astronomy in Germany and the INAF Bologna Observatory of Astrophysics and Space Science in Italy. "This makes quasars visible across billions of light-years, allowing us to observe them from the very early universe. Studying quasars helps astronomers understand how the first galaxies formed and evolved, and how the supermassive black holes at their hearts grew to such enormous sizes," Belladitta said. The Dún Aonghasa supermassive black hole is about 90 times more massive than the one at the center of our Milky Way. A TRANSFORMATIVE EPOCH It dates to one of the universe's most dramatic and transformative epochs. After the Big Bang, the cosmos cooled into a dark and neutral fog of hydrogen gas. The first stars and galaxies then began to ignite, and their intense radiation slowly burned through the fog, making the universe transparent to light for the first time. "This process was still unfolding at the time this quasar and its host galaxy were forming. It is a remarkable epoch to find such an object. The supermassive black hole powering this quasar had already grown to an enormous mass in an extremely short time, which challenges our understanding of how black holes can grow so large so quickly in the early universe," Belladitta said. One possibility is that this black hole started out small after the demise of a star that was part of the first stellar generation, but the observations indicated it was consuming material at a rate too slow to have achieved its great mass so quickly. Another possibility is that it may have been born big in a formation scenario called direct collapse. "Normally, a large cloud of gas cools and breaks up into smaller clumps that form stars. Under the right conditions, the gas could stay warm enough to limit that fragmentation, allowing much of it to flow towards the center. That gas can build up a single enormous star that quickly collapses into a black hole. That black hole would start out far more massive than the remnant of a typical first-generation star," Wolf said. The researchers said Euclid may yet spot quasars at farther distances — meaning older — than Dún Aonghasa, with theoretical models suggesting that the first quasars could potentially date to 270 million to 470 million years post-Big Bang. "So in short: this is the furthest quasar we have ever seen, but maybe not the furthest there is to find," Belladitta said.

WASHINGTON, Nov 24 : Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh has called artificial intelligence a "hinge" of history critical to US leadership, but the technology has also become key to Fed policy as officials debate whether the AI boom is a transformational moment, a source of inflation, or the harbinger of an economic meltdown.  For Warsh, who calls himself "cautiously optimistic" about what he refers to as "super intelligence," as President Donald Trump does, it may be an all-of-the-above dilemma that challenges the US central bank and his leadership of it. "This is a serious test for Warsh," Evercore ISI Vice Chairman Krishna Guha, a former New York Fed official, wrote after major US equity indexes closed last week in correction territory. They were dragged down by nervousness about AI's ability to pay off and by unease over the scandal around AI chip giant Nvidia and the brief ouster of its CEO. Recent inflation and growth data "is too hot and too strong ... But with growth dependent on AI investment and AI consumer net-worth effects, the Fed needs any weakening to remain contained," Guha wrote. "Warsh needs to balance the data with markets that suggest the forward look is cooler, and his desire to assert inflation credibility with his desire not to go down in history as the Fed chair who blew up the AI boom."

After a run that saw a political backlash against AI, a market slump, a major initial public offering, a massive corporate scandal, and a seeming rebound from it all with equity markets again surging, Fed officials are expected to follow through with a quarter-percentage-point rate increase at their December 8-9 meeting. While they do not necessarily aim to — or have any guarantee they can — slow the AI boom, many see it pushing growth beyond potential and see the need to restrain some aspects of investment and demand. "If the investment rate slows way down, then yes, I'd be less concerned that there would be overheating in the economy," Chicago Fed President Austan Goolsbee told reporters last week, likening the strain AI puts on capacity to trying to get a "pig through the python." But the impact of rate hikes on the economy "doesn't have to be sector by sector," he said. "The Fed has only one tool, which is to tighten rates ... I do think data centers are included in that business investment" and might be influenced by rising borrowing costs. 'VERY TROUBLING SIGN' Some US central bank officials have recently discussed AI. Fed Governor Lisa Cook noted possible financial risks and the likelihood that AI is already eliminating jobs, and Fed Vice Chair Philip Jefferson said AI investment is currently raising inflation, with any productivity benefits still to come. Warsh, who before taking over as Fed chief had cautioned central bankers to avoid taking sides on political issues like climate change, has called success in AI a make-or-break issue for the US.  "We are at a hinge point for the US economy, the United States' role in the world," Warsh said last week at an AI conference he commissioned, held at the San Francisco Fed. "I don't think any of us are impartial to how we want that to come out."  Increasingly, however, Warsh's colleagues see a more nuanced debate and are focused on near-term implications. The volatility has been apparent: Nvidia reversed course and rehired Jensen Huang as its chief executive officer on Monday, and stocks surged back after recent sharp losses. Politically, the country has become more divided, too, about how to balance AI's benefits and risks, the pace of construction, and concerns that the technology is moving too fast without proper oversight. "People are afraid. When the average American hears AI, they hear I'll lose my job, my kids will lose their jobs, my children's mental health, national security, some version of that," former US Commerce Secretary Gina Raimondo said on a panel with Warsh at his AI conference.  Raimondo, who currently co-chairs a nonprofit trying to ease the AI transition for workers, noted that many ballot initiatives meant to slow data-center construction were approved by voters during the recent US midterm elections. "I think that is a very troubling sign," she said. "When people are afraid they say 'stop.' I think that would be very bad for America and for them. So where I think we have to go from here is to figure out how we address people's legitimate concerns." WARSH 'BROUGHT THIS REVOLT ON HIMSELF' The Fed's role, as Warsh likes to note, is not to pick winners and losers but to guide the credit conditions in which all firms operate, in ways that affect inflation. Fed officials' view of AI investment as a source of inflation has put the Fed at direct odds with Trump, who wants the boom to roll on. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and other administration officials say rising prices are primarily the fault of still-high global oil prices that will fade as energy costs ease.  Warsh, who has defined his chairmanship partly by avoiding guidance on upcoming policy decisions, has acknowledged that AI "hits demand first," with supply and productivity improvements coming later and possibly helping ease inflation down the road. But he has not yet made the same leap as others and has avoided commenting on whether he feels the AI boom and inflation are now running hand in hand, and on how the Fed may need to respond. That question has become a key issue ahead of the next policy meeting, when policymakers are due to update their interest rate projections after a period in which the rhetoric of many of them leaned hawkish even as the election results, stock markets and other dynamics pointed to a possible slowdown. The problem for markets since the midterm elections "has not been just the prospect of an AI slowdown. It's also been that the Fed has seemingly ignored the risks and uncertainty that the post-election period has brought, and thrown caution to the wind," Macquarie analysts wrote recently. "In a way, Warsh has brought this revolt on himself, by not abandoning his own aversion to expressing forward guidance," even as the debate around what he sees as the signature economic issue of the day has become more complex.

Anthropic's shares slipped below their US$83 initial public offering price in premarket trading on Tuesday (Nov 24), a striking unraveling just days after the Claude developer's record-breaking Nasdaq debut. After briefly breaking below its offer price, the stock was last down 5 per cent at US$83.39, extending a steep retreat from its US$111.50 opening price on Nov 19. Anthropic missed out on a broad Wall Street rally driven by AI-related stocks after Nvidia reinstated Jensen Huang as chief executive on Monday. Anthropic's rapid reversal has added to concerns about stretched AI valuations and the vast sums being poured into computing infrastructure, with rising interest rates threatening to push those costs even higher. As the first frontier AI company to go public, Anthropic is widely seen as a proxy for the sector. "If we do see a slowdown in the data-centre buildout, then that obviously can impact the speed at which Anthropic can develop and therefore future revenue and therefore its valuation," said Fiona Cincotta, senior market analyst at StoneX. Anthropic is not alone among blockbuster technology IPOs in quickly surrendering early gains and falling below its offer price. SpaceX, whose US$85.7 billion June listing was the world's biggest before Anthropic, took about a month to fall below its offer price. In 2012, Facebook, now Meta Platforms, had slipped below its offer price on its second trading day. The comparisons show that a swift loss of an IPO premium is not unprecedented even for highly anticipated listings, and that an early break below the offer price is not necessarily a guide to longer-term performance.

KEY RISKS With Anthropic's shares now testing their IPO price, attention is turning to risks that could determine where the stock goes next, including insider selling, pressure from open-weight models and a potential slowdown in data-centre investments. Anthropic's IPO lock-up provisions allow certain employees and insiders to sell portions of their holdings from the first trading day, with further staggered releases tied to earnings announcements. CEO Dario Amodei and President Daniela Amodei sold more than 3.37 million shares worth over US$280 million each to the IPO's underwriters a day after the debut, according to a filing late on Monday. Anthropic's underwriters also exercised their option to buy additional shares, lifting the IPO's gross proceeds to a record US$93.5 billion, while removing a potential source of support for the stock after its debut. Anthropic also faces growing competition from cheaper open-weight AI models, which it has warned could pressure pricing. Users can download and adapt models from DeepSeek, Mistral and Moonshot AI, unlike proprietary models such as Claude, ChatGPT and Gemini, with Chinese developers in particular gaining ground globally. Huang's return could also sharpen the competitive threat to Anthropic, given his strong advocacy for open-weight AI models. Some support could emerge in the coming days as Anthropic's addition to major indexes prompts buying from passive funds. Index rebalance analytics firm Intropic estimates passive funds could buy up to 30 per cent of the shares offered by the year-end. MSCI will add Anthropic to its global standard indexes as of the Nov 30 close.

BOSTON/NEW YORK, Nov 24 : Nvidia's board undermined its claims of independence by reinstating CEO Jensen Huang before investigations into his conduct concluded, investors and corporate governance experts said on Monday. The decision is striking because the board effectively vouched for Huang's candor and fitness to lead the company before its own investigation was complete, raising doubts about whether directors had sufficient information to make an independent judgment, these people said. Nvidia said on Monday that after talks with senior US officials, its board "is confident that Mr. Huang’s reinstatement poses no national security risk." Huang resigned on November 12 after reports of extramarital affairs, including one involving a suspected Chinese spy.

The abrupt U-turn, just days after the board vowed to look elsewhere for a successor, has also drawn US President Donald Trump and his administration into Nvidia’s corporate governance. Nvidia shares closed 31.5 per cent higher on Monday even as it was becoming clear that the chipmaker's board acted under pressure from Trump and others, and the president took credit for the change. Nvidia faces investigations, including by the US Securities and Exchange Commission and the Justice Department, over issues ranging from its accounting to alleged chip smuggling. Nvidia press representatives did not immediately respond to questions for this story. The situation undercuts the board's standing, said New York City Comptroller Mark Levine, who helps manage retirement funds that hold some 5 million Nvidia shares. "They told us flatly that he would not be coming back. They have done a total 180 without any explanation, or any indication that concerns about legal and other liabilities have been resolved," Levine said in a telephone interview.  "They have proven they're not independent, and that is the defining quality that we need from any board," he said. Jan van Eck, a large Nvidia investor via the investment company bearing his name, said Huang's return likely removes uncertainty but amounts to a bet against further bad headlines. "I had expected more of a Washington DC process, including Congressional hearings, to lengthen this determination, but I guess the Administration is willing to risk that there are no more bad facts to emerge," van Eck said in an email.    QUESTIONS OF CANDOR In addition to saying Huang's return posed no national security risk, Nvidia's board said that after discussions, it was "satisfied with respect to Mr. Huang’s candor and ability to lead NVIDIA."   The company said an independent board committee is still investigating reports that Huang was targeted by a foreign intelligence effort, and said "the committee’s investigation will proceed to conclusion," with Huang's cooperation. The board has also taken steps like creating a new chief compliance officer position. Nada Kakabadse, a Henley Business School professor who follows corporate governance, said the statement left gaps. " 'Satisfied with his candor' is a strange phrase while the investigation into what he told the company is still open. The board has reached its verdict before the evidence is in," Kakabadse said.  Moreover, the board has given away much of the company's room for maneuver, she said. "It hands the board's judgment to the state. The same government that grants Nvidia's export licences now effectively vouches for its CEO. That makes the company politically dependent, and a future administration could withdraw the endorsement," she said. Nvidia board member Harvey Jones took the title of chair only this month. Until then, Nvidia was one of only two companies in the S&P 500 without a board chair, according to researcher Equilar.  Corporate governance experts previously had said the setup and the presence of many long-serving directors meant the board would have to show it could act independently.   Now, alongside relief at Huang's return, "there are sure to be questions about who is best placed to provide appropriate governance and oversight of key risks at the now-giant company at the center of a critically important global AI ecosystem," said Lindsey Stewart, Morningstar director of institutional insights. In reappointing Huang the board left those questions unanswered, Stewart said. SKEPTICISM FROM SOME LAWMAKERS US congressional committees will interview Huang on December 1. Lawmakers from both parties expressed skepticism about his return and the role of the administration. Some investors worried the political battles could overshadow Nvidia's commercial story. "Jensen’s return is not a total shock, but it does send a troubling message about the state of corporate governance in America. Certain executives are going to be held to different standards," said James St. Aubin, chief investment officer of Ocean Park Asset Management in California.   Harvard Law School Professor Lucian Bebchuk said there was no indication the board had secured the support of Nvidia’s largest shareholders, nominally the owners of the company. (Top fund firms BlackRock and Vanguard did not comment for this story.)  Bebchuk said recent policies put in place by Trump-appointed regulators make it harder for big fund firms to weigh in on corporate governance issues. Even if Huang poses no national security risks in the future, his actions to date could still entangle him and the company in costly investigations, Bebchuk said. "The board presumably feels now vindicated by the immediate stock price increase following this morning’s announcement. However, the board’s reversal of its earlier decision raises serious questions and concerns," Bebchuk said.

LONDON, Nov 24 : Britain's financial watchdog has warned technology and social media companies that AI agents offering financial services could face regulatory action, urging companies to engage early with supervisors. The statement on Tuesday coincided with Meta's launch of its Muse AI agent into the UK. Muse in the UK can perform tasks such as renewing car insurance, chasing refunds and making online purchases, but it will not initially be able to access bank account statements or provide personalised financial guidance.  The Financial Conduct Authority did not name any companies in its statement on Tuesday and directed its guidance at companies considering launching agentic products in the UK. The FCA said that simply describing a business as a technology provider does not make it exempt from financial regulation if products include regulated services such as financial promotions, advice or payment services.

Nearly two weeks after Jensen Huang stepped down as chief executive of Nvidia , the Taiwanese-American tech billionaire on Monday (Nov 23) was reinstated as CEO in a stunning comeback . Huang had stepped down earlier this month following revelations of extramarital affairs, including one with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy . His resignation plunged the chipmaker into crisis and sent shockwaves across an AI industry he helped bankroll. US stocks surged on Monday , with the Nasdaq jumping more than 6 per cent as Huang’s reinstatement drew investors back to AI-related shares after last week’s rout. Nvidia soared as much as 36.6 per cent after its board announced his return. Huang’s comeback followed strong public pressure for his reinstatement, including from US President Donald Trump, industry figures such as Tesla CEO Elon Musk and prominent venture capitalists. A petition calling for his reinstatement drew over 180,000 signatures.

In a statement, Huang said that he was honoured to return and "can’t wait to get back to work".  Videos circulating on social media showed the CEO - wearing a navy jacket instead of his signature black leather jacket - with his hand over his heart, looking up at employees gathered across multiple floors in the building.  "I’m going to be a better CEO the second time around," he said, amid cheers and applause.

Related:

Wall Street jumps back as Jensen Huang returns as Nvidia CEO

Inside the ‘war room’ that lobbied Donald Trump to bring back Nvidia’s Jensen Huang

Here’s a timeline of how the controversy unfolded and how Nvidia's share price has taken a wild ride with him. Oct 29: US investigation reported, Huang defends business dealings The New York Times (NYT) reported on Oct 29, 2026, that US authorities had investigated Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang , "who had a close relationship with Jensen Huang" - over suspicions that she had been "passing intelligence to Beijing" and helped circumvent US restrictions on advanced AI chips. The NYT report stated that US President Trump was "briefed and took no action". It also raised questions about Alice Huang’s relationship with the Nvidia CEO. Closing share price: US$213.66, 0.8 per cent down from Oct 28. Oct 30: Alice Huang suspected of having links to Chinese intelligence The next day, the Wall Street Journal published a report alleging that Alice Huang was suspected of having links to Chinese intelligence. "Investigators believed the woman, Alice Huang, was recruited based on her relationship with Jensen Huang," the WSJ report said, also attributing concerns to Singapore officials about her relationship with Huang and alleged intelligence connections. Speaking to Bloomberg News on Oct 30, Huang described Nvidia’s dealings with Singapore-based cloud computing firm Megaspeed as "normal and not unusual" and said that the company had checked that Megaspeed did not illegally divert Nvidia AI chips to China. "We've studied all their deployments of our GPUs and counted every one," Huang told Bloomberg - also describing his interactions with Alice Huang, who was "no longer with Megaspeed", as typical of those with Chinese customers and executives. That same day, Beijing rejected the espionage allegations, describing them as "groundless speculation" and an attempt to "smear China". Closing share price: US$204.64, 4.2 per cent down from Oct 29. Oct 31: Trump voices support for Huang On Oct 31, a Saturday, Trump voiced his support for Huang in the wake of the NYT report, calling him " brilliant ", adding that Washington was looking "very closely" at the issue. "I have a lot of respect for Jensen. I didn’t know about the specific thing, but I hope he’s going to be OK. He's a great, brilliant person, and we want to protect our brilliant people," Trump told reporters at his Florida residence. "We’re going to check it out very closely," he added. Huang has advised Trump on AI policy and was among the bevy of tech CEOs who joined the US leader on his visit to Beijing in May to meet Chinese President Xi Jinping.

Related:

From affair allegations to Nvidia probe: How the Jensen Huang controversy unfolded

Nvidia probe: Woman in spy scandal entered Taiwan on Hong Kong passport, say authorities

Nov 4 to Nov 5: US lawmakers seek briefing from Nvidia CEO Three senior Republican lawmakers requested a closed-door briefing from Huang over the reported intelligence allegations. In a letter dated Nov 4, House Foreign Affairs Committee chairman Brian Mast, House Select Committee on China chairman John Moolenaar and House Intelligence Committee chairman Eric Crawford asked Huang to appear before them on Nov 18. According to Reuters, the lawmakers sought information about the allegations and Nvidia's procedures for protecting sensitive information from foreign intelligence operations. Nvidia responded that its chief executive regularly meets customers and business leaders worldwide, and that its cloud customers in Asia receive ordinary business information rather than sensitive trade secrets or information affecting US national security. Closing share price on Nov 5: US$181.60, 9.3 per cent down from Nov 4. Nov 8: Huang admits his infidelity In a bombshell message to Nvidia employees dropped on a Sunday, Huang admitted that he had been "unfaithful" to his wife , following reports about his alleged relationship with Alice Huang. Huang wrote that his actions had "hurt her" and their children. "There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry." He added that he took "full responsibility for what I did and the hurt I caused" and "accepts the criticism that comes with it". He also said that he remained "fully committed to Nvidia" and "supports the independent investigation". "I am committed to protecting Nvidia and supporting America’s national security," Huang said. Following Huang's admission, Nvidia announced that its board was launching an independent investigation into whether Huang was targeted by a foreign intelligence operation. Closing share price: US$186.64 on Friday (Nov 6), 2.8 per cent up from Nov 5.

Nov 9: Trump defends Huang Following the revelations, Nvidia's stock drop wiped about US$190 billion off its market value. Meanwhile, Trump described Huang as an "honorable guy" who had "done an amazing job for our country". However, speaking to reporters, he said he had not discussed the affair allegations with Huang. "I just know he's a fine person, but you never know what is going on," he added. Chinese government officials again dismissed allegations of Chinese espionage during a routine press briefing on the same day.  "The so-called allegations of Chinese espionage are entirely baseless and amount to nothing more than smears and attempts to discredit China," said Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesperson Guo Jiakun. Closing share price: US$178.67, down 4.3 per cent from Nov 6. Nov 10: Shareholder sues Nvidia and Huang The Associated Press (AP) on Nov 10 reported that a shareholder had sued Nvidia and Huang , accusing them of deceiving investors in their responses about Huang’s affair. The complaint accused Nvidia and Huang of failing to disclose the affair and issuing false statements about Nvidia’s relationship with Singapore-based Megaspeed, which posed a “material risk” to Nvidia’s reputation and business prospects. It is common for shareholders to sue companies after unexpected share price declines. Closing share price: US$168.89, down 5.5 per cent from Nov 9.

Related:

Alice Huang in touch with Chinese spy agency during affair with Nvidia CEO: Report

US lawmakers criticise Nvidia decision to reinstate Huang as CEO

Nov 11: Alleged second affair involving Huang In another blow to Huang’s reputation, the New York Times on Nov 11 reported the tech billionaire had an extramarital affair with Kimberly Powell , the company’s vice president of health care. The report cited five people who worked at the company, and followed another report that Nvidia’s company board was preparing to oust Huang from his position. While this affair remained unconfirmed, Nvidia shares fell nearly 4 per cent in extended trading. Closing share price: US$173.73, up 2.9 per cent from Nov 10. Nov 12: Huang resigns as Nvidia CEO Huang announced his resignation as CEO of Nvidia on Nov 12, with the company’s chief financial officer Colette Kress taking over as interim CEO. Kress and longtime Nvidia engineer Ian Buck had emerged as the leading internal candidates among investors and analysts even before Huang's departure. Closing share price: US$166.19, 4.3 per cent down from Nov 11. Nov 13: US lawmakers summon Huang US lawmakers on Nov 13 summoned Huang to face their questions in December following his resignation. At this point, the scandal had wiped almost half a trillion dollars off Nvidia's market valuation, AFP reported. "Recent reports raise serious concerns about our national security and the protection of sensitive US technology," Republican Senator Tim Scott wrote on X. Scott added that he was requesting Huang and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick to testify in December before the Senate Banking Committee, which he chairs, last week. Huang is also scheduled for a closed-door interview with three House of Representatives committees on Dec 1, on threat of subpoena. Closing share price: US$162.85, 2 per cent down from Nov 12.

Nov 16: Huang discusses comeback with allies Citing people familiar with the matter, the Financial Times on Nov 16 reported that Huang was considering a comeback as Nvidia’s CEO. One source told FT that they were putting together a "war room" of Silicon Valley executives to lobby for Huang’s return and also try to garner support from the White House. The campaign to reinstate him as CEO saw support from tech industry leaders and many of Nvidia’s employees. SpaceX and Tesla boss Elon Musk and Tim Sweeney, CEO of video game maker Epic Games, were among thousands of people who signed an online petition calling for Huang to return to the company. Trump told reporters that he would welcome Huang’s return at Nvidia. "I would certainly not mind seeing that. "I think he learned a big lesson." Closing share price: US$156.14, 4.1 per cent down from Nov 13. Nov 17: Nvidia chair says board will not rehire Huang Nvidia chairman Harvey Jones on Nov 17 said the board did not intend to reinstate Huang as CEO , despite the latter saying that he was ready to return. Hours before Nvidia’s quarterly results were released on Nov 17, Huang said he "would be honoured" to come back as CEO if the board decided his return would be in the best interest of shareholders and employees.

Jensen Huang reacts as employees applaud his return to office after Nvidia reinstated him as the company's CEO, in Santa Clara, California, US on Nov 23, 2026, in this screengrab obtained from a social media video. (Photo: Zhengzhong Tu/via Reuters)

However, Jones quashed that possibility on a call with analysts after Nvidia's earnings were released, saying the board would take the search for a new CEO "very seriously" and would consider internal and external candidates. Nvidia doubled its revenue in its third quarter to more than US$115 billion, the company reported on Nov 17, exceeding analysts' expectations.  Closing share price: US$155.46, 0.4 per cent down from Nov 16. Nov 20: Nvidia shares fall further, Trump calls for second chance Anthropic’s much-hyped arrival on Wall Street could not arrest Nvidia's slide. The record US$81 billion listing failed to dispel growing worries about the sector’s massive investments and sky-high evaluations. Traders were also spooked by the US Commerce Department's move to close a loophole allowing Chinese companies to access Nvidia's powerful AI chips remotely, adding to worries that a new Democratic-led Congress will impose further restrictions on the sector. Meanwhile, Trump again sang Huang's praises, saying that the former CEO should be "given a second chance". "I would love to see him be back. You have one of the truly most brilliant minds in the world, and where is he going to go?" Trump told reporters. "I think that I would love to see Jensen be given a second chance."

BENGALURU, Nov 24 : Will Thomas has played Fantasy Premier League (FPL) for over 15 years. Last season, the AI he built finished above him for the first time. "That was a bit of a surreal moment. I thought, 'oh my God, I'm being beaten by my own creation'," he told Reuters. According to industry research, Thomas is one of around 245 million people who play fantasy sports, where players take the role of manager or coach and build a virtual team made up of athletes whose real-life performances earn them points. Englishman Thomas is also CEO and founder of Scoreline.ai, which delivers subscriber-based content including data, insight and analytics designed to help players manage their fantasy sports teams.

Among its products is Fantasy Football Hub, which has around 60,000 paying subscribers and focuses on FPL - the official fantasy competition of the English Premier League. FPL offers match tickets and replica kits as prizes and had over 13 million registered teams in the 2025-26 season. Scoreline.ai's purpose-built model finished in the top 0.5 per cent of those teams, ranking 67,829th in the world. "There are still human managers beating it, but it's getting harder to do," said Thomas, who has a PhD in team leadership at the University of Sussex. HOW DOES AI MATCH UP TO THE BEST HUMAN PLAYERS? A Reuters analysis of nine FPL teams, seven of which were run on the directions of AI chatbots, showed that the chatbot teams scored an average of 499 points in the first eight gameweeks of the 2026-27 FPL season. The chatbot teams which Reuters analysed were operated by Scout Digital, a sports marketing firm that gives each separate chatbot the same instructions every week and, in most cases, has a staff member log in to carry out its decisions. Their performances were in line with the average human benchmark of 502, but about 75 points below the average of the top 1,000 human players, showing that AI has improved sharply but has not yet caught up to the best. Reuters' analysis found chatbots still fall short of the best players on judgment calls such as captaincy picks, which earn double points, even as they match the top managers' discipline on transfers. Scout Digital said newer versions of each AI model are used as they are released. As a control, Scout Digital also has a team titled Scout Statto, which is managed by the firm's co-founder Simon Gold and run without the use of AI tools. "So far, we're two seasons in and the improvement we've seen is huge," said managing director Mike Lewis. "In 2025-26, Scout Statto comfortably won. This season is looking neck and neck." WHERE COULD HUMANS HAVE THE EDGE? Daniel Groos, head of AI at Groos Analytics, who built the open-source forecasting model OpenFPL, said the hardest question remains whether a player will even be in action on any particular gameweek and not dropped, rested or injured. Jonas Sand Labakk, the 2023-24 FPL champion, said that is where human discretion is essential. "Where you need human input is the expected minutes for players, because rotation, injuries and managerial choices are where I think the models miss the most," he told Reuters. Groos added that overall, machines have an advantage because humans tend to be influenced by a spectacular performance, media narratives or a favourite player. The chatbot teams make about as few transfers as the best human managers, and the gap in transfer volume is small. The chatbot teams' captain picks trail those of the top 1,000 human players. They also leave more points on the bench than the typical manager. The top 1,000 do not play against the grain. They own more popular players than the average manager, not fewer, which undercuts the idea that beating the field takes contrarian bets. Thomas also argues that the machines are weakest at the start of a season, when new managers and players give the models little data, and that fans of specific teams may have a slight insight advantage. However, the early numbers do not clearly show that. The chatbot teams Reuters analysed were level with the official average in gameweek 1 of this season, pulled ahead in gameweek 2, and had dipped just below it by gameweek 8. USING AI AS A CO-PILOT, NOT AN AUTOPILOT While some predict a future where fantasy sports become a battleground purely for competing versions of AI, Groos does not expect the human element to disappear completely. "The winning formula may turn out to be neither human intuition nor AI-based insights, but a combination of both," he said. Labakk echoed that, adding: "I think the best possible way is an engaged manager with the models rather than an AI with the models." That is how Marcus Adebayo, 34, a software project manager from South London, uses Gemini. He lets it do the "structural heavy lifting" but picks the team himself. "Treating it as a co-pilot works brilliantly, provided you're honest enough to admit that when the plane hits turbulence, it's usually because you grabbed the controls," he said. Beginning this season, FPL features its own conversational AI assistant titled FPL Companion.

TOKYO, Nov 24 : The Bank of Japan will likely raise interest rates several more times to fight inflation, but its rate-hike plans may face political headwinds next year due to weak consumption, former central bank policymaker Seiji Adachi said on Tuesday. While government fuel subsidies have moderated price pressure on households, inflation is likely to stay above the BOJ's 2 per cent target next year as firms pass on rising raw material costs, Adachi said in an interview with Reuters. "Concern over rising inflation is strong, so the BOJ is not done with rate hikes yet," he said, projecting the central bank will raise its policy rate to 1.5 per cent from the current 1.25 per cent either in December or January. The BOJ could then raise rates further to 1.75 per cent or 2.0 per cent next year to forestall the risk of an inflation overshoot, Adachi said.

But he warned that soft consumption may complicate the BOJ's rate-hike plans, with recent data showing signs of weakness in household spending. "Consumption has been weakening this year and moving below recent years' trend," with rising living costs and higher interest rates prodding households to save rather than spend, Adachi said. Signs of weak consumption may spur dovish premier Sanae Takaichi's administration and her reflationist aides to push back against further rate hikes, he said. "If consumption stays weak, it could prove hard for the BOJ to justify steady rate hikes. Falling stock prices won't help either," said Adachi, who retains contact with incumbent policymakers and some of Takaichi's economic advisers. "The pain from higher rates may hit households first through higher mortgage rates, which the administration may not feel happy about," Adachi said. "How far the administration is willing to tolerate could be key" to the pace and timing of any BOJ rate hikes next year, he added. During his five-year stint at the BOJ board until 2025, Adachi took part in the central bank's exit from a massive decade-long stimulus in March 2024 and subsequent rate hikes. With stubbornly high energy costs and rising import prices from a weak yen adding to inflationary pressures, the BOJ raised its policy rate to 1.25 per cent in September after delivering a hike in June — a shorter interval than the roughly twice-a-year hikes seen in 2024 and 2025. BOJ Governor Kazuo Ueda has signalled the bank's readiness to keep raising rates to prevent inflation from deviating above its 2 per cent target. A majority of analysts polled by Reuters expect the BOJ to raise rates in December and follow up with another hike by end-March. Many see the terminal rate at around 1.75 per cent or 2.0 per cent. Wary of triggering a fresh selloff in the yen and government bonds, Takaichi's administration has held off on publicly criticising the BOJ's recent rate hikes and hawkish signalling. But two dovish BOJ board members dissented to the September rate hike on concern over weak growth and consumption. Japan's economy unexpectedly shrank in the July-September quarter as consumption slumped, though Ueda last week played down the weakness as due to temporary factors such as bad weather.
